title: ICICI Pru Signature Secure: A Five-Year Single-Premium ULIP With a Guaranteed Maturity Benefit of Up to 140% of Premium
summary: ICICI Prudential Life launched ICICI Pru Signature Secure on June 11, 2026, a single-premium, five-year unit linked plan whose maturity payout is the higher of fund value or a guaranteed maturity benefit of up to 140% of the premium paid, with no premium allocation or policy administration charges.
description:
ICICI Prudential Life Insurance has launched a unit linked insurance plan, or ULIP, that pairs market-linked investment with a guaranteed payout at maturity. The product, called ICICI Pru Signature Secure, was launched on June 11, 2026, according to reports from IBS Intelligence and CafeMutual. It is a single-premium plan, meaning the customer pays once at the start, with a five-year policy term.

A ULIP combines life insurance with investment. The premium, after charges, is used to buy units in funds that can hold equity, debt or a mix, and the value of those units rises and falls with markets. Traditional ULIPs offer no guarantee on the fund value at maturity, which is why savers who are uncertain about markets often avoid them. Signature Secure adds a floor. At maturity the policyholder is paid the higher of two amounts: the value of the fund, or a guaranteed maturity benefit that the company states can be up to 140 per cent of the premium paid.

The company gave an illustration. A 45-year-old who invests Rs 5 lakh would have a sum assured of Rs 6.25 lakh, and the guaranteed maturity benefit would be Rs 7 lakh. The Rs 7 lakh figure equals 140 per cent of Rs 5 lakh, which is simple arithmetic and shows the top of the quoted range. The sum assured of Rs 6.25 lakh is 125 per cent of the premium. The reports do not explain how the guaranteed percentage is determined for different ages or premiums, and the phrase up to 140 per cent means that some customers may receive a lower guarantee. If the fund performs well, the payout can exceed the guarantee, since the policyholder gets whichever is higher.

The plan provides life cover during the term. If the policyholder dies, the nominee receives the benefit defined in the policy, which the coverage describes in terms of a chosen sum assured. The coverage does not set out the exact death benefit formula, so buyers should read the policy document for it. The reports also said that the plan has no premium allocation charge and no policy administration charge. These are two of the charges that commonly reduce the amount invested in a ULIP. However, the coverage did not list other charges such as fund management fees and mortality charges, nor the minimum premium or the fund choices, so the full cost of the product cannot be assessed from these reports.

The company's Chief Product Officer, Vikas Gupta, was quoted on the product in the launch coverage. Earlier summaries called Signature Secure the first ULIP in India with a guaranteed element. The sources reviewed here do not establish that claim, so the first-of-its-kind label should be treated as unconfirmed.

How should a saver think about a product like this? A five-year horizon is short for equities, and a guarantee that is expressed as a multiple of the premium paid over five years has an implied annual return, which for 140 per cent is roughly 7 per cent a year before considering that the sum is paid at the end. That calculation is an approximation using compound growth and ignores tax, and the company does not describe the guarantee as a rate of return. It nonetheless gives a useful way to compare the guarantee with the alternatives, such as fixed deposits, debt funds or traditional savings policies.

The product also has to be viewed against the regulatory background. India's life insurance sector has been reported to be dealing with changes to commission and expense rules, the Bima Sugam digital marketplace and norms linking executive pay to policyholder outcomes. Such changes affect how products are designed and sold, and they increase the importance of clear disclosure, particularly for products with guarantees whose terms may be misunderstood.

Before buying, a customer should check the surrender and lock-in terms, the conditions under which the guarantee applies, whether the guarantee is only payable if the policy runs to full term, how it is backed by the insurer's balance sheet, and what tax treatment applies to maturity proceeds under current rules. Those details determine how the product compares with other options, and none of them appears in the coverage reviewed here, so the policy brochure and benefit illustration are the right place to find them.

One further point concerns the word guarantee. A guaranteed maturity benefit is only as strong as the insurer's ability to pay it, and it applies on the terms of the policy, for example if the policy is held to maturity. A customer who surrenders early would ordinarily receive a surrender value that can be lower than the premium paid, and the coverage does not say how this plan treats early exit. Buyers should therefore treat the five-year term as a commitment and ask for the surrender value table before paying the single premium.
image_alt: Life insurance policy documents and a pen representing a new ULIP product (illustrative)
key_points: ICICI Pru Signature Secure is a single-premium unit linked plan with a five-year term, launched on June 11, 2026.
At maturity the policyholder receives the higher of the fund value or a guaranteed maturity benefit of up to 140% of the premium paid.
In the company's example, a 45-year-old paying Rs 5 lakh gets a sum assured of Rs 6.25 lakh and a guaranteed maturity benefit of Rs 7 lakh.
The plan has no premium allocation charge and no policy administration charge, according to the reports.

Other charges, minimum premium and the fund options were not stated in the coverage, and the description of it as India's first ULIP with a guarantee comes from earlier summaries and should be treated with caution.
why_it_matters: Buyers who like equity-linked products but fear a poor outcome over a short horizon may be drawn to a guarantee, yet the value depends on the charges and conditions that sit behind it. The headline guarantee is a floor on the maturity payout, not a promise of a particular return.

title: EY Forecasts a 108% Combined Ratio for UK Motor Insurers in 2026, Their Deepest Loss of the Soft Cycle, With Premiums Needing to Rise 16% Over Two Years
summary: EY's July 2026 analysis forecasts a UK motor net combined ratio of 108% in 2026 after 102% in 2025 and 98% in 2024, with a partial recovery to 103% in 2027 and premiums expected to rise 4% in 2026 and 12% in 2027 as insurers restore margins.
description:
The UK motor insurance market is heading for its weakest underwriting result of the current soft cycle, according to analysis from EY published on July 23, 2026. EY's net combined ratio, which measures claims and expenses as a share of premiums after reinsurance, was 98 per cent in 2024, a profitable year. EY's estimated final figure for 2025 is 102 per cent, a small underwriting loss, and its forecast for 2026 is 108 per cent, which means roughly £1.08 paid out in claims and expenses for every £1 of premium earned. For 2027 it forecasts a partial recovery to 103 per cent, which is still above 100 per cent. The 2025 result was therefore a small underwriting loss rather than a break-even year, and EY expects losses to continue through 2027 on current assumptions.

The cause is a squeeze from two sides. On the premium side, EY says rates fell by almost 12 per cent during 2025, and that this drop is feeding through to earned premium, the premium recognised as cover is provided, in 2026. Insurance Business UK quoted EY as saying the lower rates from 2025 compound claims inflation. On the claims side, EY expects total net claims to rise by 4 per cent in 2026 and 5 per cent in 2027. Claims frequency is expected to stay broadly stable, and EY and the other coverage point to the average cost of a claim as the primary driver of claims inflation. Repair, labour and vehicle costs are the main pressure points, and oil price volatility and supply chain disruption could raise repair, parts and logistics costs further. None of the coverage reviewed gives a specific percentage for repair cost inflation.

The scale of the claims bill gives context. The Association of British Insurers reports that motor insurers paid out £11.9 billion in 2025, and that vehicle damage claims were £7.5 billion of this, or 63 per cent. Because vehicle damage is the largest component, changes in repair costs have an outsized effect on results. Moody's, in a separate report on UK insurers, said that motor claims inflation had fallen to mid-single-digit levels and that vehicle technology is raising repair costs, since electric vehicles can cost more to fix and battery damage can increase the chance that a car is written off. That is consistent with EY's forecast of 4 to 5 per cent growth in net claims, although the two organisations measure different things.

EY expects the premium response to be large. It forecasts that premiums will rise by 4 per cent in 2026 and 12 per cent in 2027, which is about 16 per cent over two years. Adding two annual changes of 4 and 12 per cent gives a compounded figure of about 16.5 per cent, so 16 per cent is a fair summary. Dan Beard, UK insurance partner at EY, said consumers should expect higher motor insurance premiums over the next two years as insurers look to restore margins. The Insurance Business UK article also cited Defaqto data showing that motor premiums rose 3.6 per cent in the first half of 2026, which suggests the turn in prices has begun. For drivers, the practical point is that the low renewal prices of the last year or two may not last, and that comparing quotes at each renewal matters more when the market is changing direction.

Beard's comments describe a market that is diverging. He said that UK motor insurers are navigating a difficult combination of lower earned premium income and persistent cost inflation, that 2026 could be the toughest year of the current soft cycle, and that the market is becoming more polarised, with the gap between stronger and weaker performing insurers widening. The Insurance Business UK article adds that consolidation and merger activity are reshaping competition. A soft cycle is a period when insurers compete on price, and it normally ends when losses force a rise in rates. EY's numbers suggest that the turning point is arriving in 2026 and 2027.

EY also sets out a risk to its own forecast. Geopolitical pressure could push net combined ratios up by a further 5 to 10 per cent beyond the forecasts, according to the press release. The coverage does not define how that range is calculated, so it should be read as a warning about the direction of risk, not a precise number. For comparison, the Insurance Business UK article cited Oxbow Partners in June 2026 as forecasting that UK motor operating profit would fall from £2 billion in 2025 to £1.3 billion in 2026, with the combined ratio rising from 89 per cent to 95 per cent. That is a smaller deterioration than EY's, and the two combined ratios are not directly comparable because they are defined differently, but both point in the same direction.

For insurers, the incentives are clear. After a second and third year of underwriting losses, according to CollisionWeek, insurers have a direct motive to scrutinise repair spend more closely, which affects the garages and body shops that carry out repairs. The full text of that article was not accessible for this review, so the specific effects on repairers are not described here. What can be said from the EY figures is that insurers will use pricing, tighter claims management and underwriting selection to restore profitability.

What to watch is the pace of premium increases in the second half of 2026, whether claims inflation stays within the mid-single-digit range, and whether the partial recovery that EY forecasts for 2027 materialises. The forecast is conditional on claims cost trends, and EY says so. The UK motor market is therefore likely to be defined less by cheap prices over the coming two years than by insurers trying to bring their combined ratios back below 100 per cent.
source_name: EY UK press release (July 23, 2026), Insurance Business UK (July 23, 2026) and CollisionWeek (July 27, 2026)
image_alt: Cars on a UK road representing motor insurance market conditions (illustrative)
key_points: EY estimates the UK motor net combined ratio was 98% in 2024, about 102% in 2025, and forecasts 108% in 2026 and 103% in 2027, so the market is expected to be loss-making in each of those last three years.
Premiums fell by almost 12% during 2025; EY expects them to rise 4% in 2026 and 12% in 2027, about 16% over two years.
Net claims are expected to rise 4% in 2026 and 5% in 2027, with claims frequency broadly stable but the average cost per claim rising because of repair, labour, vehicle, parts and logistics costs.
EY says geopolitical pressure could push net combined ratios 5% to 10% above its forecasts, and UK insurance partner Dan Beard called 2026 potentially the toughest year of the current soft cycle.
The ABI says motor insurers paid out £11.9 billion in claims in 2025, of which vehicle damage was £7.5 billion, or 63%.
why_it_matters: A combined ratio above 100% means insurers pay out more in claims and expenses than they collect in premiums, so they must either raise prices, cut costs or accept losses. EY's forecast therefore points to higher motor premiums for drivers over the next two years after a period when prices fell, and to a growing gap between stronger and weaker insurers.

title: Munich Re Cut Its 2026 Reinsurance Revenue Target to €38 Billion on Softer Pricing, Cutting Retrocession and Sidecars While Holding Its €6.3 Billion Profit Guidance
summary: After CFO Andrew Buchanan said on July 22, 2026 that Munich Re was reviewing its P&C reinsurance revenue outlook, the group confirmed on August 7 that it expects €38 billion of reinsurance revenue and €62 billion of group revenue, down €2 billion each, while keeping its €6.3 billion net result guidance.
description:
Munich Re's July warning about its reinsurance revenue was an early sign of how a softening market reshapes the world's largest reinsurer. On July 22, 2026, Insurance Business reported, citing Börsen-Zeitung, that Munich Re was reviewing its property and casualty reinsurance revenue outlook because softer market conditions were pressuring growth. Chief financial officer Andrew Buchanan was the source. Two weeks later, the company confirmed the cut in its half-year results. The sequence is useful because it separates revenue, which is falling, from profit, which the company says is not.

The July warning followed one in May. At that time, Munich Re said that reaching its 2026 P&C reinsurance revenue target of €40 billion (about US$46.7 billion) had become harder. Buchanan told Börsen-Zeitung that the factors behind that assessment had not gone away, and said the company would take a very close look at the business in the pipeline for the third and fourth quarters, adding that this would determine the guidance given to the market. Life and health reinsurance revenue was, in his words as reported, broadly on track, because that business is insulated from the price declines affecting property and casualty.

The first-quarter results, published in May, show the profit side. Net profit was €1.714 billion, the P&C reinsurance combined ratio was 66.8 per cent, and the full-year net income target of €6.3 billion was maintained. At April renewals Munich Re's written volume fell 18.5 per cent to €2.0 billion as it declined business below its minimum return thresholds, and risk-adjusted prices fell 3.1 per cent. Morningstar DBRS, cited in the article, said property catastrophe pricing had fallen 10 to 15 per cent since January 2026, and that global reinsurance capital had grown to US$805 billion. Jefferies analysts estimated that only a loss event exceeding US$100 billion would reverse the softening cycle.

The company's own actions show how it is responding. According to Insurance Business, it exited two sidecar vehicles, declined to renew a catastrophe bond, reduced retrocession cover, and retained peak peril exposure on its own balance sheet instead of transferring it. Its Solvency II ratio was 292 per cent at the end of March, compared with an internal target corridor floor of 200 per cent. The review of revenue was, the article stressed, separate from the profit target: a reflection of premium volume effects, not of weaker underwriting profitability. Its Ambition 2030 strategy targets a return on equity above 18 per cent through to the end of the decade.

The confirmation came on August 7, 2026. Insurance Business reported that Munich Re cut its July renewal volume by 9.1 per cent and declined business that did not meet its pricing requirements. The risk-adjusted price decrease was 5.5 per cent, with the business concentrated in North America, South America, Australia and global clients. Terms and conditions stayed largely stable, and higher loss cost estimates, mainly from inflation and other loss trends, were mostly offset by price adjustments. Munich Re said the risk-adjusted price level remained good despite the decline, and expected favourable price levels at January 2027. The Guy Carpenter global property catastrophe rate-on-line index fell 16 per cent across 2026, the steepest annual fall since the late 1990s, according to the article.

On that basis the company revised its revenue expectations: reinsurance revenue to €38 billion from €40 billion, and group insurance revenue to €62 billion from €64 billion. Net result guidance of €6.3 billion was unchanged. The second-quarter P&C reinsurance combined ratio was 68.9 per cent against 61.0 per cent a year earlier, though the article notes the prior-year figure benefited more from a release of reserves. Major-loss expenditure was €191 million after retrocession and before tax, or 4.9 per cent of net insurance revenue, against an expected value of 18 per cent, made up of €54 million of natural catastrophe losses and €137 million of man-made major losses. Gallagher Re data cited in the article showed five consecutive below-average quarters for major losses, with about US$46 billion of global insured catastrophe losses in the first half against a ten-year average of US$64 billion.

The group result was strong. Net result was €1.25 billion in the second quarter and €3.92 billion for the half year, up from €3.18 billion. Insurance revenue in P&C reinsurance fell to €4.04 billion from €4.51 billion because of the lower renewal volume. Retrocession cover was cut from US$1.55 billion to US$600 million. Life and health reinsurance net result was €489 million, helped by what the company described as its largest single longevity transaction, which transferred €4 billion of pension liabilities. The investment result was €3.16 billion, a 5.5 per cent return on average market value. The solvency ratio stood at 304 per cent on July 1, up from 298 per cent at the end of 2025. Chair Christoph Jurecka said the company was able to manage the market cycle in property-casualty reinsurance from a position of strength.

What came afterwards matters for readers. A later article on this site reported that Munich Re raised its 2026 profit target to €6.6 billion after a preliminary third-quarter result, with the final figures due on November 12. That combination, lower revenue and higher profit, is exactly the pattern the July warning described: a reinsurer willing to write less business at lower prices while claims stay below expectations. The risk is a large loss event, which would test the reduced retrocession protection the company now carries.
source_name: Insurance Business (July 22 and August 7, 2026), citing Börsen-Zeitung and Munich Re
image_alt: Corporate office buildings representing a global reinsurance business (illustrative)
key_points: On July 22, 2026 CFO Andrew Buchanan told Börsen-Zeitung that the factors behind May's warning had not gone away and that Munich Re would look closely at the pipeline for the third and fourth quarters, which would determine guidance.
On August 7 Munich Re lowered its reinsurance revenue expectation to €38 billion from €40 billion and group revenue to €62 billion from €64 billion, while keeping net result guidance at €6.3 billion.
At July renewals Munich Re cut volume by 9.1% and accepted a 5.5% fall in risk-adjusted prices; at April it cut volume 18.5% and prices fell 3.1%.

P&C reinsurance combined ratio was 68.9% in the second quarter against 61.0%, with major losses at 4.9% of net insurance revenue against an expected 18%, and retrocession cover was cut from US$1.55 billion to US$600 million.
The Solvency II ratio was 304% on July 1, 2026, against a 200% minimum, and later reports note that preliminary third-quarter figures led the group to raise its profit target to €6.6 billion.
why_it_matters: Munich Re is a bellwether for the reinsurance cycle. Its choice to shrink premium rather than accept lower prices shows how a soft market works: revenue falls first, while profit holds up as long as claims stay below expectations.
